planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed past 65°F and frost danger has passed, setting a sturdy 5-6 foot trellis at planting since the vigorous vines reach 8-10 feet.

directions: This Haywood County, North Carolina heirloom gets its name from the pink blush that develops on the pod's blossom end as the seeds inside reach full maturity, a trait unique among the region's many greasy bean strains. Like other greasy beans, the smooth hairless pods take on a glossy sheen when cooked, and the plump white seeds are prized for both fresh shelling and dried leather britches preparation. Train vines onto a tall, well-anchored trellis early, since this is an unusually vigorous and heavy-yielding climber. Pick pods at 4-5 inches for the best snap texture, or let the last flush dry fully on the vine for seed saving and winter storage beans.

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil is thoroughly warm, providing a tall trellis since the vines climb 7-9 feet and need consistent moisture through flowering and pod set.

directions: This bean traces to the Cades Cove community in the Great Smoky Mountains, where families including the Olivers, Shields, and Tiptons grew it before their valley was absorbed into the national park in the 1930s; home gardeners carried the seed out with them and it eventually reached wider heirloom circulation through Seed Savers Exchange. The hairless, shiny pods are the hallmark of the greasy bean group, distinguishing it visually from fuzzy-podded snap beans at a glance. Harvest pods young, around 4-5 inches, while the seeds inside are still plump but not yet hardened, for the best snap texture and flavor. A portion of the crop can be left to dry fully on the vine for shelling, storage, and seed saving.

planting.note: Direct sow in mid-to-late summer so the roots size up during cool fall weather; thin seedlings to their final spacing once true leaves appear.

directions: Despite the common name, this is botanically a rutabaga, not a true turnip, and traces to 1876 when brothers Adin and Elihu Macomber brought home seed from the Philadelphia Centennial Exhibition and planted it in Westport, Massachusetts, where it has remained a South Coast regional specialty ever since. The large white roots, often blushed green or purple at the shoulder, develop a mild, sweet flavor that many growers describe as sweet enough to eat raw, distinguishing it from sharper standard turnips. Roots continue to bulk up through cool fall weather and improve in sweetness after light frost, so delay harvest until nights are consistently cold. Store harvested roots in a cold, humid root cellar or refrigerator, where they keep for months.

planting.note: Plant bare-root while still dormant in late winter to early spring, in deep well-drained soil with a compatible pollinator nearby; a vigorous rootstock helps this historically uneven bearer settle into more consistent annual crops.

directions: First noted in the town of Hubbardston in central Massachusetts in the early 1800s and formally recorded by 1832, this apple became one of the most widely planted varieties across the northeastern United States through the 19th century, prized enough that the town still features paired apples on its official seal. Fruit is medium to large with a distinctive red-striped skin over yellow-green background color, and the firm, aromatic flesh suits fresh eating, baking, and cider blending equally well. Trees are notorious for variable fruit quality from site to site, so flavor can range from excellent to merely good depending on soil and climate. Fruit ripens late September into early October and keeps reasonably well in cold storage through early winter.

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil has warmed past 55°F, in blocks of at least 4 rows for reliable wind pollination; northern New England's short, cool season is this variety's natural strength.

directions: Developed from Abenaki Calais and related northern flint stock to improve yield and stalk standability, Garland is an 8-rowed flint corn bred specifically for the short, wet, cool growing conditions of the northeastern United States. Ears run 6-8 inches long and come in solid yellow or solid red depending on the seed lot, growing on sturdy 5-6 foot stalks that hold up well against wind and early fall storms. Like other northern flint corns, the hard glassy kernels grind into flavorful meal for cornbread and polenta, and the shorter season makes it a reliable choice where longer-maturing dent and sweet corns struggle to finish. Harvest for grain once husks dry and kernels have hardened fully on the stalk.
